civic_principles_card.group: HOW POWER IS BUILT AND LIMITED

principles.name: Rule of Law
principles.means: No one is above the law, not even the people who make it.
principles.look_for_it_when: someone powerful is held to the rules, or tries to dodge them.

principles.name: Limited Government
principles.means: Government can only do what the Constitution allows.
principles.look_for_it_when: someone says the government went too far.

principles.name: Separation of Powers
principles.means: Power is split among three branches, each with its own job: make laws, carry out laws, judge laws.
principles.look_for_it_when: the fight is about which branch gets to act.

principles.name: Checks and Balances
principles.means: Each branch can block or limit the others.
principles.look_for_it_when: there's a veto, an override, an impeachment, or a court striking something down.

principles.name: Federalism
principles.means: Power is divided between the national government and the states. When they clash, valid federal law wins.
principles.look_for_it_when: it's the nation against a state.

principles.name: Judicial Review
principles.means: Courts can strike down a law or action that breaks the Constitution.
principles.look_for_it_when: a court decides whether something is constitutional.

principles.name: Popular Sovereignty (consent of the governed)
principles.means: Government's power comes from the people, and it rules only with their agreement.
principles.look_for_it_when: people give, or take back, their support for a government.

principles.name: Representative Government
principles.means: The people elect officials to make decisions for them.
principles.look_for_it_when: the issue is voting, elections, or who speaks for whom.

principles.name: Natural Rights
principles.means: Every person is born with rights (life, liberty, property) that government exists to protect.
principles.look_for_it_when: a right is treated as something you're born with, not something government hands out.

principles.name: Individual Rights (civil liberties)
principles.means: Freedoms government can't take away, like speech, religion, press and assembly.
principles.look_for_it_when: a personal freedom is limited, defended, or expanded.

principles.name: Equal Protection
principles.means: The law must treat people equally.
principles.look_for_it_when: a group is treated differently, shut out, or separated by law.

principles.name: Due Process
principles.means: Government must follow fair steps before it takes your life, liberty, or property.
principles.look_for_it_when: someone is arrested, held, or punished. Ask whether it was fair.

documents.label: Document 16
documents.source: Source: political cartoon, Pennsylvania Gazette, 9 May 1754. Attributed to Benjamin Franklin.
documents.alt: A woodcut inside a black border. A snake is cut into eight separate pieces, each labeled with a colony or region's initials. Below it, in large capital letters: JOIN, or DIE.

documents.label: Document 16b
documents.source: Source: Benjamin Franklin, Pennsylvania Gazette, 9 May 1754 (adapted)
documents.text: “…The Confidence of the French in this seems well-grounded on the present disunited State of the British Colonies, and the extreme Difficulty of bringing so many different Governments and Assemblies to agree in any speedy and effectual Measures for our common Defence and Security; while our Enemies have the very great Advantage of being under one Direction, with one Council, and one Purse.”

documents.label: Document 4
documents.source: Source: Miantonomo, Narragansett sachem, speaking to the Montaukett on Long Island, c. 1642. Recorded by an English listener and printed later in Great Native American Speeches.
documents.text: Brothers, we must be as one as the English are, or we shall all be destroyed.

paragraph: In 1754, each of Britain's colonies in North America had its own government, and war with France was coming on the frontier.
Document 4 shows the same idea from the other side, when Miantonomo warns, “we must be as one as the English are, or we shall all be destroyed.”
This matters because people split into separate governments could not defend themselves against an enemy that acted as one.

pieces.text: Document 16b shows the problem when Franklin blames “the present disunited State of the British Colonies.”
Outside the documents, I know that at the Albany Congress in 1754, the delegates approved Franklin's Plan of Union, but the colonial assemblies turned it down.
The civic principle at stake is federalism: power divided between one central government and the separate colonies, which would become states.
Franklin printed this article in the Pennsylvania Gazette.
Franklin's cartoon shows a snake cut into pieces above the words “JOIN, or DIE.”
The colonies should have worked together.

The principle is named out loud, from the card. Tap CIVIC PRINCIPLES if you need the list.
tasks.reasoning: Franklin's own words prove the problem, the Albany Plan shows the union failing, and federalism names what was at stake.

documents.text: “By marriage, the husband and wife are one person in law: that is, the very being or legal existence of the woman is suspended during the marriage, or at least is incorporated and consolidated into that of the husband: under whose wing, protection, and cover, she performs everything…”
